summary.text: The Intertropical Convergence Zone is the belt circling Earth near the thermal equator where the northeast and southeast trade winds meet, a stretch sailors called the doldrums.
Thunderstorms powered by solar heating lift air upward there and draw the trade winds in, so the zone appears as a wet band of clouds around the globe.
Its position shifts with the seasons, and that shift brings many equatorial nations wet and dry seasons instead of cold and warm ones.

facts.label: Earlier name
facts.value: Intertropical Front, used from the 1920s to the 1940s

facts.label: Calm spells
facts.value: Could strand sailing ships for days or weeks

items.prompt: In the 1700s a sailing ship crossing the equator drifts for days in hot, muggy, almost windless weather. Where has it ended up?

options.label: In the horse latitudes, far from the equator
Where the two trade-wind belts meet
In the calm eye of a hurricane
Under the polar jet stream

items.explain: Near the equator the northeast and southeast trade winds converge, and winds there are slight; sailors named this calm belt the doldrums.

items.prompt: Seasons in many equatorial countries are shaped by the yearly north-south movement of this zone. What kind of seasons does that movement create?

options.label: Cold and warm seasons, like higher latitudes
Long polar days and polar nights
Wet seasons and dry seasons
Seasons of strong and weak tides

items.explain: As the zone moves, rainfall changes drastically, giving the tropics wet and dry seasons rather than cold and warm ones.

items.prompt: The zone swings much farther north and south over continents than over open sea. Why?

options.label: Mountains on land push the winds aside
Winds over oceans are always stronger
Earth's rotation has less effect over water
Oceans have a greater heat capacity than air over land

items.explain: Because the oceans hold heat better than the air over land, the seasonal migration is more prominent over land.

items.prompt: The zone sits north of the equator, and a southeast trade wind blows across the equator into the Northern Hemisphere. What does it become?

options.label: A southwest wind
A northeast wind
A northwest wind
It stays a southeast wind

items.explain: Earth's rotation (the Coriolis effect) changes the wind's direction as it crosses the equator, turning the southeast trade into a southwest wind.

items.prompt: Tropical cyclones need spinning air near the surface to get started. What does this zone supply toward that?

options.label: Cold, dry air sinking from high up
Low-level spin from changing wind speed and direction
Steady winds blowing in a single direction
Clear skies that let the sea surface heat up

items.explain: Low-level vorticity is one of the requirements for tropical cyclones, and the zone provides it because winds there change in direction and speed (horizontal wind shear).

items.prompt: In summer the zone drifts away from the equator toward subtropical latitudes. Why do tropical cyclones form more easily within it then?

options.label: The trade winds stop blowing completely
The sea surface becomes colder
The Coriolis force grows stronger there
The days become much shorter

items.explain: Farther from the equator the Coriolis force increases, which makes tropical cyclones more likely to form within the zone.

paragraphs.heading: Where the trade winds meet
paragraphs.text: The Intertropical Convergence Zone, or ITCZ, is the belt where the trade winds from the northeast and from the southeast run into each other. It wraps around the planet close to the thermal equator, though its exact position shifts with the season. It shows up as a band of clouds, mostly thunderstorms, circling the globe near the Equator. Sailors called it the doldrums or the calms, after its dull, windless weather.

paragraphs.heading: What drives it
paragraphs.text: The zone is built by air moving upward, mostly inside thunderstorms powered by the Sun's heat. As that air climbs, it pulls more air in toward it, and this inflow is the trade winds. North of the Equator the trades come from the northeast and head southwest; south of it they come from the southeast and head northwest. The ITCZ marks the wet, rising branch of a circulation called the Hadley cell, while its dry, sinking branch lies over the horse latitudes.

paragraphs.heading: A belt that wanders
paragraphs.text: Through the year the zone drifts north and south, roughly tracking the thermal equator. The drift is larger over land, since the oceans hold more heat than the air over land does. Over the sea the zone is sharper and its yearly swing is gentler, because ocean temperatures limit where its storms can grow. Sometimes two zones form, one on each side of the Equator, usually with one stronger than the other and a thin ridge of high pressure between them.

paragraphs.heading: Wet and dry seasons
paragraphs.text: Because the zone moves, many countries near the Equator get wet and dry seasons instead of the cold and warm seasons found farther from it. The timing of rain there is traditionally explained by the zone following the Sun north and south. That holds well over the equatorial oceans, but over the continents the zone and the heaviest rain can come apart. Changes in the zone that last longer can bring severe drought or flooding to places nearby.

paragraphs.heading: A nursery for storms
paragraphs.text: One of the six things a tropical cyclone needs is spinning air near the surface, and the ITCZ supplies it, since the wind there changes in direction and speed. As the zone moves away from the Equator during each hemisphere's summer, the Coriolis force, the turning effect of Earth's rotation, grows stronger, which makes cyclones more likely to form inside it. In the tropical north Atlantic and the eastern tropical north Pacific, disturbances called tropical waves travel along the zone and stir up more thunderstorms.

paragraphs.heading: Becalmed
paragraphs.text: Inside the zone the average wind is light, unlike the belts to the north and south where the trades blow in. In the eighteenth century, as more ships crossed the Equator, sailors named this calm belt the doldrums. When wind was the only real way to move a ship across an ocean, getting stuck there in hot, muggy air could be deadly, and calm spells could hold a ship for days or weeks. Racing and leisure sailors today still try to cross it fast, because its unpredictable winds and weather can hold them up.

paragraphs.heading: Danger in the air
paragraphs.text: The zone's storms matter for planes too. In 2009 Air France Flight 447, flying from Rio de Janeiro to Paris, crashed while passing through a series of large ITCZ thunderstorms, and no one on board survived. Ice building fast on its airspeed sensors set off a chain of human errors that brought the plane down. Most aircraft on these routes steer around the biggest storm cells with no trouble.
